Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

escape verb

someone’s notice or memory

also it escapes me, slip one’s mind, escape notice, go unnoticed, I’ve lost track, it slipped my mind to

classical

Cic. Rep. 2, 12: id quod fugit Lacedaemonium Lycūrgum (Lewis & Short)
Catull. 10.29
Cic. Att. 7.18.3: dē Dionysiō, fugit mē ad tē anteā scrībere (Lewis & Short)
Traupman p. 108: fūgit mē (+ infinitive)

mē fugit

phrase: fugiō with the accusative of the person; the thing as subject, or an indirect question

it escapes me, I don’t notice or remember

The thing that escapes one is the subject: fugit mē ratiō (Catull. 10.29). Also nōn mē fugit, I am well aware.

Other words

  • fallō, fallere, fefellī, falsum — escape the notice of; go unnoticed

    verb, third conjugation · also used · classical · Cic. de Or. 1.255 (Lewis & Short); Liv. 22.33.1: quī per biennium fefellerat

    In this sense mostly impersonal in Cicero and Caesar: neque hoc tē fallit, you are well aware of this. Of a person, to go unnoticed (Liv. 22.33.1). Its everyday sense is to deceive.

Examples

  • fugit mē ratiō

    I got mixed upCatull. 10.29

  • tantō silentiō in summum ēvāsēre ut nōn custōdēs sōlum fallerent, sed nē canēs quidem, sollicitum animal ad nocturnōs strepitūs, excitārent

    they reached the top so quietly that they slipped past not only the guards but even the dogs, creatures alert to noises in the night, without waking themLiv. 5.47.3

See also escape, forget, remember.
